title: The lichens that left the city
teaches: How lichens vanished from smoky cities, how they were used to map sulphur in the air, and how they came back once the smoke ended
summary: **Lichens vanished from industrial cities in the nineteenth century.** Naturalists in Manchester and Paris noticed bare trunks where lichens had been.
**Nylander blamed the air in 1866.** He called lichens a gauge of how healthy the air was.
**Sulphur dioxide from coal smoke was the main cause.** It dissolves in the rain a lichen soaks up and turns it acid.
**Lichens differ in how much they can bear.** Bushy beards go first, leafy kinds next, and a few grey crusts hold on in all but the dirtiest air.
**Hawksworth and Rose turned this into a scale in 1970.** The lichens on a tree told the average sulphur in the air around it.
**Clean-air laws brought the lichens back.** As coal smoke ended, they returned to cities, the toughest first.
**A new pollution changed which ones came back.** Nitrogen from traffic and farms favours bright orange and yellow lichens.

blocks.text: In 1859 the Manchester botanist Leo Grindon wrote that the lichens which had once grown on the trees and walls around the town were gone, and blamed the smoke of the mills. A few years later the Finnish lichenologist William Nylander, whom lesson 10 met fighting Schwendener, looked for lichens in the Luxembourg Gardens in the middle of Paris and found almost none, though old records listed many. In 1866 he wrote that lichens are a gauge of the health of the air, a phrase lichenologists still quote.

Over the next century the same pattern was seen in every industrial city of Europe and North America. Near the centre, tree trunks were bare, or coated only in a thin green film of single algae.[^moths] Further out, a few grey crusts appeared. Further still came leafy lichens, and only in the countryside the long bushy beards and big leafy lobes that the old botanists had recorded everywhere.

The cause was mainly **sulphur dioxide**, a gas given off by burning coal, which contains a little sulphur. In the air it dissolves in water droplets to make an acid. Lesson 10 explained why lichens are exposed: they have no roots and no waxy skin, and they soak up rain and dew over their whole surface, taking in whatever is dissolved in it. Each time a lichen wets, its algae are bathed in acid. The gas damages the green pigment the algae use to catch light, and a lichen whose algae cannot make sugar starves.

A plant is protected by its waxy leaves and draws its water from the soil, where the acid is partly neutralised. So the trees could survive in air that killed the lichens on their bark. Lichens also grow so slowly that they cannot replace what they lose. That made them sensitive gauges: a lichen on a tree has been sampling the air for years.

In 1970 David Hawksworth and Francis Rose published a scale for England and Wales. Using measurements of sulphur dioxide from monitoring stations and lists of the lichens on trees near them, they divided the country into ten zones. In the cleanest zone grew the large leafy lungwort lichen and long beard lichens. In the dirtiest, nothing but the green algal film. In between, each zone had its own set of lichens, and a person who could recognise a few kinds could read the average winter sulphur in the air from any tree.

The scale was cheap, it needed no equipment, and it measured the air over years rather than on the day of a reading. Schoolchildren used it in national surveys, sending in lists of the lichens on the trees near their homes and schools; a similar survey run since 2008 uses lichens to map nitrogen.

blocks.caption: The lichens on a tree in central London over a century, with the sulphur dioxide in the air. The sulphur figures are rough yearly averages; the lichens are a model.

blocks.text: In December 1952 a smog over London killed thousands of people in a few days. The Clean Air Act of 1956 that followed, with later laws, moved homes and factories off coal, and power stations were built away from cities with tall chimneys and, later, scrubbers that strip sulphur out of the smoke. Sulphur dioxide in London fell from hundreds of micrograms in each cubic metre in the 1950s to a few today, a fall of about a hundredfold.

The lichens came back. Surveys in London in the 1970s and 1980s found species returning to parks that had been lichen deserts for a century, the toughest first, then leafy kinds, and by the 2000s some of the bushy beards. A lichen that grows a millimetre or so a year cannot return quickly, and a spore or fragment has to arrive from somewhere cleaner, so the recovery lagged the air by years.

The lichens that came back were not quite the old ones. In the 1990s, ecologists noticed that bright orange and yellow lichens, such as the common orange wall lichen, were spreading fast on city trees and on twigs in farmland. These lichens thrive on nitrogen, and the air was now carrying a great deal of it, as nitrogen oxides from traffic and ammonia from livestock and fertiliser. Some of the most sensitive lichens of clean air are harmed by the same nitrogen, so they remain rare.

So lichens are now used to map nitrogen in much the way they once mapped sulphur. The rule Nylander stated still holds, with a new pollutant: what grows on a tree tells you what has been in the air around it.

blocks.caption: Four questions on lichens and city air
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why are lichens more sensitive to sulphur dioxide than the trees they grow on?
choices: They soak up rain over their whole surface and have no waxy skin
They need more sulphur than trees
items.why: Whatever is dissolved in rain goes straight into a lichen. A tree's waxy leaves and its roots in the soil protect it.

items.ask: On Hawksworth and Rose's scale, what does a tree with only a green film of algae tell you?
choices: The air has a lot of sulphur dioxide
items.why: In the dirtiest zones no lichen survived, only single algae.

items.ask: Why did lichens return to London years after the air cleaned?
choices: They grow slowly and must arrive from cleaner places
The Clean Air Act did not take effect for decades
They need smoke to start growing
items.why: A lichen must reach the tree as a spore or a fragment and then grow slowly. Recovery lagged the air.

items.ask: Why have orange and yellow lichens spread in recent decades?
choices: They thrive on nitrogen from traffic and farms
items.why: Nitrogen oxides and ammonia feed these lichens, which now mark a different kind of pollution.

moths.title: Lichens and moths
moths.text: Bare, sooty trunks also changed the peppered moth. On pale lichen-covered bark the speckled moth was hidden from birds; on blackened bark the rare dark form survived better and became common around industrial cities. As the air cleaned and lichens returned, the speckled form came back too.
